slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by naming the payoff of polyhedral convexity. Instead of quantifying over infinitely many possible supporting objects, many claims reduce to finitely many faces, inequalities, and multipliers. The lecture will keep one linear program visible so every abstract statement can be tested against active constraints and residuals.

slides.title: Polyhedral Applications Map
slides.notes: Position the section as a bridge from representation theory to optimization practice. The common mechanism is finite face structure. Once the class sees a polyhedron as finitely many faces, the later applications to optima, multipliers, and closed images become different readings of the same finite combinatorics.

slides.title: Active Constraints
slides.notes: Make active constraints the first concrete certificate. At a point of a polyhedron, most inequalities are slack and irrelevant to the local face. The constraints that tie as equalities define the face, and at a nondegenerate planar vertex two independent active lines are enough to pin down the point.

slides.title: LP Vertex Certificate
slides.notes: Use the moving level lines to show why an optimum sits on an exposed face. For a polygon the face is often a vertex, but the certificate is not just the picture. It includes feasibility of all inequalities, equality for the active set, and absence of a feasible recession direction that improves the objective.

slides.title: Finite Certificates
slides.notes: Translate polyhedral applications into a certificate ledger. Feasibility is a finite row check. The active set is a finite equality pattern. Optimality is a finite cone-membership statement for the objective normal. This is the section's practical theme: the geometry is convex, but the certificate is linear algebra.

slides.title: Normal Cone Multipliers
slides.notes: Introduce the normal cone as the compact language for active multipliers. At a polyhedral point, the cone is generated by finitely many active normals. A linear objective is optimized at that point when its normal belongs to this cone, which is exactly the multiplier certificate in geometric form.

slides.title: Closedness And Images
slides.notes: Use this slide to explain why polyhedral hypotheses strengthen conclusions. Projection is a common source of closure trouble for general convex sets, but a polyhedron projects to another polyhedron in finite dimension. That finite description keeps the resulting set closed and makes existence or duality arguments cleaner.

slides.title: Piecewise Linear Models
slides.notes: Connect sets and functions by moving to epigraphs. A piecewise linear convex function has a polyhedral epigraph because finitely many affine lower bounds define it. The active pieces at a point play the same role as active inequalities, and their slopes generate the local subgradient information.

slides.title: Sensitivity Normal Fan
slides.notes: Use sensitivity as another application of finite face structure. The objective normal does not choose a new optimizer continuously at every angle. Instead it moves through finitely many normal cones. Inside one cone the optimizer is stable, and crossing a boundary explains exactly when the active face changes.

slides.title: Numerical Checker
slides.notes: Tie the slide to the notebook check. The selected optimum must pass three finite tests: all slacks nonnegative, active slacks zero, and objective normal compatible with the active cone. If a test fails, the failure is informative because it says whether feasibility, activity, or optimality was incorrectly claimed.

slides.title: Learner Lab
slides.notes: Frame the lab as active-set debugging. Students should perturb one ingredient and then explain the new face structure before trusting the numerical answer. The certificate should say which constraints are active, whether all slacks have the right sign, and whether the objective is bounded in the displayed direction.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the section theme: polyhedral convexity is powerful because it leaves finite evidence. The student should be able to point to rows, active equalities, normal cones, or multiplier vectors. That habit prepares the following material on systems of inequalities and alternatives.
